questions.question: What is a struct in Go, and how do you define one?
questions.title: Struct Definition
questions.direct_answer: type Name struct { fields }. A struct is a composite of named fields with independent types — Go's only user-defined aggregate. Zero value: every field at its zero value.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Struct Definition beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its complexity or failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: type Name struct { fields }. A struct is a composite of named fields with independent types — Go's only user-defined aggregate.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A struct definition names a group of fields, each with its own type:

```go
type User struct {
    Name string
    Age  int
}
```

Creating values: the composite literal with field names (the only style that survives field reordering), positional (fragile — don't), or the zero value:

```go
var u User            // zero: Name "", Age 0 — both executed-verified
u2 := User{Name: "Al", Age: 30}
```

The zero value is fully usable — no constructor needed, no nil state, no 'uninitialized struct' concept. A User with empty name and age 0 is as valid as any other. That design choice (zero values are meaningful) shapes Go: functions document whether the zero value works (bytes.Buffer: yes; strings.Builder: yes) and constructors are the exception for types needing setup, not the rule.

Structs are the only way to bundle heterogeneous data in Go — no classes (methods attach separately), no records, no unions. What they give up in expressiveness they return in simplicity: comparable when fields are comparable (verified: User{Name:"a",Age:1} == User{Name:"a",Age:1} is true), copyable wholesale (assignment copies all fields), and laid out predictably (the compiler orders fields to minimize padding, but you control it by ordering fields yourself).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    L[struct literal] --> K[keyed: Name field names — safe]
    L --> P[positional: every field in order — fragile]
    L --> Z[var u User — zero value: all fields at zero]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The two mechanics interviews probe for:

Field layout: Go stores fields in declaration order, inserting alignment padding as needed — but (unlike C) the compiler MAY reorder to optimize... actually Go's spec guarantees NO reordering: fields stay in written order with padding between. Two consequences: (1) identical field sets in different orders can differ in size — order large-to-small to minimize padding; (2) you can predict the layout for binary formats (with fixed-size types) — though encoding packages exist for that.

Struct literals and the unnamed-struct trick: anonymous structs (struct{ X, Y int }) are valid types — comparable, usable in APIs — and appear in JSON fixtures and tests. The position dependence of unnamed literal fields makes them a maintenance hazard in real APIs (adding a field breaks every positional literal at compile time, which is the safe failure; the unsafe one is silent misalignment when types match).

The zero-value design has an exception worth knowing: maps and slices inside structs are nil after zero-value creation — the struct itself is 'ready' but its reference-typed fields need their own make(). The composite ready-check (reflect or manual) distinguishes 'struct zero' from 'struct ready', and constructors exist exactly to bridge that gap for types whose reference fields are load-bearing.

questions.question: What are struct literals, and what are the ways to create a struct value?
questions.title: When would you use Struct Definition in a real project
questions.direct_answer: Three: keyed (User{Name: "Al", Age: 30}) — the safe default; positional (User{"Al", 30}) — every field, in order, fragile; var u User — the zero value, every field at zero.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Remember: Three: keyed (User{Name: "Al", Age: 30}) — the safe default; positional (User{"Al", 30}) — every field, in order.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The three forms, in the order you should reach for them:

Keyed literal — field names explicit, any subset of fields (missing = zero):

```go
u := User{Name: "Al", Age: 30}
v := User{Name: "Bo"}   // Age: 0 — deliberate
```

The two properties that make it the default: self-documenting (field names in the call) and refactor-safe (reorder fields, add fields — keyed literals keep compiling with the same semantics).

Positional literal — every field, in exact order:

```go
w := User{"Al", 30}   // legal but fragile
```

Compiles only with ALL fields present; breaks at compile time when fields are added (good) or reordered (the compiler catches the type mismatches — mostly). Its honest niche: small, frozen structs — image.Point{1, 2}, a coordinate pair that will never grow. In API code, keyed only.

Zero value — no literal at all:

```go
var u User   // Name: "", Age: 0 — executed-verified
```

The zero value is the cheapest and often the most correct: for structs designed for it (Buffer, Builder, sync types), the zero value IS the ready value — the constructor-free style the standard library proves works at scale.

The one form that doesn't exist: mandatory constructors. Go's answer is 'the zero value should be enough; constructors are for the types that can't achieve that' — so most struct creation in real Go is keyed literal or var, and New() functions appear only where invariants genuinely require setup.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    L[struct literal] --> K[keyed: Name field names — safe]
    L --> P[positional: every field in order — fragile]
    L --> Z[var u User — zero value: all fields at zero]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The keyed/positional distinction has a compile-time safety story worth knowing precisely. Positional requires: exact field count, exact order, and every field — the compiler enforces all three. So 'add a field' breaks every positional literal in the codebase with clear errors — you find them all at once. The DANGEROUS case is reordering two same-typed fields: Name/Name2, both string — a positional literal compiles fine with values silently swapped. That's why style guides ban positional except for nameless pairs.

Keyed has its own subtle rule: duplicate field keys (User{Name: "a", Name: "b"}) are a compile error in struct literals — unlike map literals where later keys win. The stricter rule exists because a struct literal is an expression evaluated once, not a mutable assignment sequence.

The zero-value form's mechanics: var u User is a declaration — the struct storage exists at declaration point (stack if it doesn't escape, heap if it does — escape analysis decides), fields already zeroed by the memory allocator (Go's allocator returns zeroed memory, so 'zero value' isn't an extra initialization pass — it's the allocation's default state, and constructors that set everything pay no extra cost for the zeroing they overwrite).

The anonymous-struct corner: var u struct{ X, Y int } — a complete type defined inline in the variable's type. It compares, it assigns, it works — and its niche is when a shape is used exactly once (a test's fixture, a JSON envelope in one handler). Anything used twice deserves a name; the unnamed struct is a local dialect, not a building block.

questions.question: Can you compare two structs in Go?
questions.title: a common mistake when using Struct Definition
questions.direct_answer: Structs are comparable with == when ALL their fields are comparable — field-by-field, in order. Any slice/map/function/chan... channels ARE comparable... any slice, map, or function field makes == a compile error.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Structs are comparable with == when ALL their fields are comparable — field-by-field, in order. Any slice/map/function/chan..

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
== on structs works exactly when it can: all fields comparable → element-wise comparison; any non-comparable field (slice, map, function — note: channels and interfaces ARE comparable) → compile error:

```go
User{Name:"a", Age:1} == User{Name:"a", Age:1}   // true — all fields equal, executed
User{Name:"a", Age:1} == User{Name:"b", Age:1}   // false — any field differs

type Doc struct { Tags []string }
// Doc{...} == Doc{...}   // compile error: Doc is not comparable
```

The comparison is field-by-field in declaration order — the same == semantics each field type has. Two consequences: it's shallow (pointer fields compare by pointer, not pointee), and it's all-or-nothing (the compiler refuses the WHOLE struct if ANY field can't compare — no partial equality).

For structs that can't ==: reflect.DeepEqual (runtime, panics on some cycles, slow — the test-time tool) or slices/maps-based comparisons or a hand-written Equal method (production code — explicit, fast, version-able semantics). The honest interview progression: == when the compiler allows it; Equal() method when equality is a domain concept with its own definition (case-insensitive names? nil-vs-empty normalization?); DeepEqual in tests only.

The copy semantics pair: assignment (u2 := u) copies all fields — shallowly (reference fields share their pointees) — so == and copy are consistent: equal structs stay equal after independent assignment until a mutable shared field changes under one of them.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    L[struct literal] --> K[keyed: Name field names — safe]
    L --> P[positional: every field in order — fragile]
    L --> Z[var u User — zero value: all fields at zero]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why the strictness? Go's design: == must be cheap, well-defined, and hashable (usable as map keys) — so any type with == gets the full suite. A slice can't == because 'same contents or same identity?' has no right answer cheaply; a struct holding one inherits the ambiguity — the compiler stops it at the boundary instead of picking a semantics.

The map-key corollary, worth stating because it's a standard follow-up question: comparable structs are valid map keys. map[User]int — Go hashes all fields. The rules propagate: change a field to []string and the map breaks too (compile error, not a runtime surprise).

The shallow comparison detail: type P struct{ U *User; N int }; P{u1, 1} == P{u2, 1} compares the POINTERS u1 == u2, not *u1 == *u2. Two structs with identical pointed-to data are unequal if they hold different pointers — the same identity-vs-equality distinction Go made for channels and interfaces, applied through struct fields. When that's wrong for your domain, the Equal() method is where you define it.

reflect.DeepEqual exists because tests need structural equality over graphs (documents with slices containing slices) — but it answers a different question than == (deep structural equivalence, nil-vs-empty distinct in some cases) and its performance (reflection over every field) and edge semantics (cycles panic) keep it out of production paths. The test/production line is the practical answer interviewers want: == for the cheap hashable types, Equal() for domain semantics, DeepEqual for test fixtures.

questions.question: How do you embed a struct in Go, and what does embedding give you?
questions.title: compare Struct Definition with an alternative
questions.direct_answer: type Admin struct { User; Level int } — the inner struct's fields and methods are PROMOTED: admin.Name and admin.Greet() work directly. Composition, not inheritance — no polymorphism, no virtual dispatch.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: type Admin struct { User; Level int } — the inner struct's fields and methods are PROMOTED: admin.Name and admin.Greet() work directly.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Admin] --> EMBED[User embedded]
    EMBED --> PF[field: Name promoted]
    EMBED --> PM[method: Greet promoted]
    A --> OWN[field: Level — depth 0]
    PF --> LOOKUP[name lookup: depth 0 first, then depth 1]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The mechanics of promotion — how the compiler actually resolves a.Name: name lookup walks the struct's fields at increasing depth. Level and User are at depth 0 on Admin; Name is at depth 1 (inside User). A reference to a.Level finds depth 0; a.Name finds nothing at depth 0, descends into the embedded User, finds Name — promoted. Two rules keep this unambiguous: a shallower name always wins (a shadowing outer Name hides User's), and two same-named things at the SAME depth are an ambiguity — usable only through the explicit path (a.User.Name).

The promoted METHOD is a wrapper, not an alias: a.Greet() compiles to a.User.Greet() — a real method value with the receiver being the inner struct. That's why the method's own promoted lookups resolve within the INNER type's scope (a.Greet() using u.Name reads User's field even if the outer had its own Name at depth 0 — the receiver's type governs).

The composition pattern this enables — the standard-library proof: bufio.Reader embeds io.Reader (an INTERFACE — embedding works for interfaces too, promoting the interface's methods as compile-time-checked delegation); ReadSeeker-style composed interfaces embed io.Reader + io.Writer. The idiom: embed what you delegate to; the promotion IS the delegation; the interface satisfaction follows for free.

The inheritance-vs-composition payoff, stated once: embedding solves 'reuse the inner's fields/methods and satisfy its interfaces' without any of inheritance's problems (fragile base, deep hierarchies, accidental override). The cost: no polymorphism — when you need an inner-typed value to behave differently per outer type, that's an interface + method on the outer — the Go-shaped answer to the same problem inheritance was solving.

questions.question: What is the difference between embedding and a regular named field?
questions.title: debug a problem involving Struct Definition
questions.direct_answer: Embedding promotes the inner's fields/methods to the outer (a.Name works) and composes interface satisfaction. A named field keeps everything behind the field name (a.user.Name) and satisfies nothing through the outer.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Embedding promotes the inner's fields/methods to the outer (a.Name works) and composes interface satisfaction.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Same inner type, two declarations, completely different reach:

```go
type Admin struct {
    User          // embedded: promoted access
    Level int
}
type Manager struct {
    user User      // named: namespaced access
    Level int
}

a.Name          // works — User's field promoted
m.user.Name      // required — user is a namespace
a.Greet()        // works — promoted method
m.user.Greet()   // required
```

Interface satisfaction differs exactly the same way: Admin (with Greet promoted) satisfies Greeter; Manager does not — its user does, but the interface check happens on the outer type's method set.

Choosing between them is an API-design question with a clean answer: embed when the outer IS-A-USER for interface purposes (the composed type should satisfy the inner's interfaces — Logger embedded in App so App satisfies Logger) and when the promoted surface is wanted (unqualified access to the inner's API). Name the field when the inner is a component, not an identity — a Config struct holding a Logger is 'has-a logger': you want cfg.Logger.Infof explicit, the composition hidden, and the outer's API kept small.

The overriding/shadowing semantics also differ: embedding's promotion can be shadowed (outer redeclares Name — inner still reachable via a.User.Name); a named field can't conflict at all (the field name IS the namespace). And the JSON-visible difference: embedded struct's fields flatten into the outer's JSON object; named struct's nest under its key — serialization shape often decides the declaration in API-layer structs.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Admin] --> EMBED[User embedded]
    EMBED --> PF[field: Name promoted]
    EMBED --> PM[method: Greet promoted]
    A --> OWN[field: Level — depth 0]
    PF --> LOOKUP[name lookup: depth 0 first, then depth 1]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The two declarations compile to the same memory layout — an embedded field IS a field (its name is the type name: a.User and m.user are equally real storage). Every difference is in the compiler's NAME RESOLUTION and METHOD SET rules — which is why the comparison is an API-design question, not a data-structure question.

Name resolution on the embedded form is the depth-walk described in the previous deep; on the named form it's one level and stop. The interesting cross-rule: an outer type can embed the SAME inner twice via different paths (one embedded, one named) — no ambiguity, because each path has a distinct name.

Method-set composition on embedding: the outer's method set gains the inner's promoted methods — and ONLY for interface satisfaction purposes; calling still routes to the inner. This is where 'embedding an interface' differs subtly from 'embedding a struct': embedding io.Reader as a field (unnamed, interface type) — the outer satisfies Reader, AND the implementation is whatever was assigned to the field — runtime delegation with compile-time checking. That's the pattern in io packages (bufio.Reader embedding io.Reader: the wrapper satisfies the interface while forwarding calls to whatever concrete reader was embedded). Named-field embedding of an interface is impossible — the interface type only has methods, nothing to promote as fields.

The design lesson the difference teaches: Go splits 'reuse and expose' (embed) from 'use and contain' (name) — one mechanism, two declarations, an explicit choice. Languages with inheritance conflate them; Go makes the composition relationship visible in the struct definition itself, and reviewers read intent directly from which form was chosen.
